title: Med Spa Injector Commission Structure: Plans, Tiers and Credit Rules (October 2026)
summary: Build a med spa injector commission structure that holds up at payroll: base plus percentage, tiers, discounts, package credit and who gets the sale.
body_markdown:
## What a Typical Med Spa Injector Commission Structure Pays


Most injectors are paid a base (hourly or salary) plus a percentage of the revenue from their own treatments, with a smaller number on pure hourly pay. The percentage you see quoted depends heavily on who is quoting it and what it is measured against.


Pabau, a software vendor,[describes commissions of 10% to 20%](https://pabau.com/blog/should-med-spas-pay-commission/) on services performed, usually on top of an hourly wage. Zenoti's staffing guide, which draws on its own customer benchmarks,[reports 25% to 40% of injectable service revenue](https://www.zenoti.com/en-uk/thecheckin/medspa-staffing-guide) for NP, PA and RN injectors, with the top of the range going to experienced injectors with their own patient base. The same guide suggests keeping total provider compensation within 30% to 35% of the revenue that provider generates.


Both are vendor sources, and neither is a salary survey. Read the gap between them as a warning about definitions. A 15% commission on collected revenue after product cost is a very different offer from 30% on the menu price of the service. Before you compare your plan with anyone else's, compare what the percentage is applied to.


## Base Plus Commission, Hourly or Pure Commission?


Base plus commission is the default because it gives a new injector a floor while the schedule fills and gives an established one a share of the upside. Pure hourly and pure commission each fit a narrower situation.


Model Works when Watch for


Hourly only A new injector is building a book, or you want the lowest compliance risk No reason to fill open chairs or rebook; strong producers leave


Base plus commission Most clinics, from one injector to a team Base set so high the commission stops mattering


Commission only Experienced injectors with their own patient base Cash-flow swings; injectors may push volume over fit


Bonus on practice or personal targets States where commission on medical services is restricted Targets nobody can explain; payouts that feel arbitrary


Hybrid clinics have the hardest version of this. An injector who spends half the week on neurotoxin and filler and half on weight-loss or hormone visits does not generate revenue in a way one percentage describes well. That is a reason to set different rules for different parts of the menu rather than one blanket rate.


## Flat or Tiered: Graduated vs Stepwise


A flat rate pays the same percentage on every dollar, which makes it simple to explain and audit. A tiered plan raises the rate as production grows. The mistake is saying "tiered" and stopping there, because there are two different plans behind the word.


In a graduated plan, each band pays its own rate and only the dollars inside a band earn that band's rate. In a stepwise plan, the top band reached sets the rate for every sale in the period. Here is the same set of bands, 25% up to $15,000, 30% from $15,000 to $25,000 and 35% above that, applied to an injector who produces $28,000 in a month:


Plan Calculation Commission


Flat 30% $28,000 x 30% $8,400


Graduated tiers $15,000 x 25% + $10,000 x 30% + $3,000 x 35% $7,800


Stepwise tiers $28,000 x 35% $9,800


The stepwise plan pays $2,000 more than the graduated one for the same work, and it creates a cliff: the sale that crosses $25,000 reprices every sale before it. That is a strong motivator in the last week of the month and a source of arguments in the first week of the next. Graduated plans are gentler on margin and easier to defend when someone asks why a single appointment moved their check.


Also decide when the tiers reset. Monthly is the common choice, but a quarterly reset smooths out the slow season, and an injector who had a strong December should not start January from zero feeling punished. Whatever you pick, put the reset period in the plan.


## Should Commission Be Calculated on List Price, Net Price or Collected Cash?


Calculate on the net price the patient paid for the service, so the discount comes out before the percentage goes on. If the commission is calculated on the menu price, the practice absorbs the discount and then pays the injector as if it had not been given.


Take 40 units of neurotoxin listed at $600 and sold at 20% off. The patient pays $480. At 25%, commission on net price is $120 and on list price is $150. That $30 difference is small once and large across a promotion month. It also changes behavior: when the injector is paid on list price, nothing stops them from offering a discount on a package the practice would rather not run.


Two refinements are worth deciding in advance:


- **Prepaid and banked items.** A patient who prepaid for a package at a discount has already had the discount reflected in the price. Paying on the full pre-discount price would double count it.
- **Product cost.** Some plans pay on revenue after the cost of the product, which protects margin on expensive injectables. If you track costs by lot, as covered in our guide to[injectable inventory tracking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-injectable-inventory-tracking) , this is possible. Without it, the plan will be argued about, so use net price and keep it simple.


## Who Gets Credit: The Seller or the Provider?


For anything sold in one visit and delivered in the same visit, the seller and the provider are the same person and there is nothing to decide. The question shows up when they are different people, and in a med spa that is common.


The three situations that cause nearly all of the credit disputes:


- **Walk-in retail.** A patient stops at the front desk, chats with a nurse injector for two minutes about a serum, and buys it with no appointment. Without a way to credit that sale to someone, the clinician who made the recommendation gets nothing and stops making them. Clinics that pay product commission need a "sold by" field on the sales screen that front desk staff can fill in, or leave blank when no clinician was involved.
- **Packages.** A six-session package is sold once and delivered over months. The person who closed the sale and the person who treats may not be the same.
- **Re-engagement.** A coordinator texts a lapsed patient, the patient books, and an injector treats them. Someone did the chasing.


There is no universally right answer, only a consistent one. Pay the seller if you want the incentive to land on closing. Pay the delivering provider if you want it on the work. Many clinics split, with a small seller credit at the sale and the main commission at delivery. The trap to avoid is a plan that says "commission on packages" without saying which of these it means.


## Package Credit: Pay at the Sale or at Each Session?


Paying at the sale rewards whoever sold; paying at redemption rewards whoever delivers and keeps the payout matched to revenue the practice has earned. Both are defensible, and they produce different cash timing for the injector.


On a $1,800 six-session package at 25%, paying at the sale is $450 up front. Paying at redemption is $75 per session as each one is delivered. The second approach lines commission up with when revenue is recognized, which matters if you also track the liability for unused sessions, a topic we cover in[our guide to VIP memberships, beauty banks and patient wallets](https://decodahealth.com/blog/setting-up-vip-memberships-beauty-banks-and-patient-wallets) .


Whichever you choose, settle refunds. If session four is refunded, the payout that session produced should reverse. Without that rule, the injector keeps commission on treatments the practice was paid nothing for, and the correction becomes a conversation nobody wants to have with a good employee.


## Memberships and Renewals: Credit That Does Not Vanish


Membership revenue recurs, so the credit has to recur too. Decide whether the injector who enrolled the member is paid on the first month only, on every renewal, or on a defined number of renewals, and attach the seller to the membership record rather than to a single payment.


This is where plans break during a software switch. Memberships that move over without a seller attached have no one to pay, and the provider who built that member base watches the commission disappear for no reason of their own. When you migrate, check seller attribution on active memberships against a list you trust, location by location, and decide whether payments made since the switch should be credited back. It is much easier to catch this in the first pay period than after three.


Price changes matter as well. If you raise rates on existing members, the commission base moves with them, as we describe in[our post on membership price increases](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-membership-price-increase) .


## Can Two People Share Credit for One Sale?


Yes, but only if your system supports it, and many do not. Plans that say "the front desk and the injector both get credit" fall apart when the checkout screen takes exactly one name per line item.


If your tool takes one seller per item, you have three workable options: credit the clinician who made the recommendation and cover the front desk through a monthly team bonus, credit the person who closed and pay a flat referral amount outside the commission system, or write separate rules for each part of the menu so the answer is automatic. What does not work is promising a split and then reconciling it by hand in a spreadsheet, which is how the file called "commissions_final_v4" gets created.


## Legal Checks Before You Publish the Plan


Three issues come up repeatedly, and none of them is solved by the percentage you choose.


**Fee-splitting and corporate practice rules.** Some states restrict percentage-based pay tied to medical services, and the rules depend on how the practice is owned and who employs the provider. Our guide to[med spa commissions and fee-splitting](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-front-desk-commission-guide) explains where the line tends to fall for retail, memberships and medical treatments, and our[med spa legal checklist](https://decodahealth.com/blog/how-to-open-a-med-spa-legal-checklist) covers ownership structure. Have a healthcare attorney in your state review the plan.


**Overtime.** For non-exempt employees, commissions count toward the regular rate. Under[29 CFR 778.117](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/778.117) , commissions are pay for work time however they are calculated, so overtime has to account for them.


**Classification.** A contract that says "independent contractor" does not settle it. The Department of Labor's[fact sheet on employment relationships](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/13-flsa-employment-relationship) says the test is economic reality, meaning whether the worker is in business for themselves or depends on you for work. An injector who works your schedule, on your patients, in your rooms, usually looks like an employee.


## Writing the Plan Down So Payroll Close Is Boring


A plan that holds up fits on one page and answers each of these questions in a sentence. If you cannot answer one, that is where the next dispute will come from.


- What is the percentage applied to: list price, net price, or collected cash?
- Which parts of the menu earn commission, and at what rate?
- Flat, graduated or stepwise, and when do tiers reset?
- Who is credited on a walk-in sale, a package, a membership and a recall booking?
- What happens on a refund, a void or a chargeback?
- When are commissions paid, and from which report?


Put the answers into your staff handbook, as in our post on[setting up med spa staff SOPs](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-staff-sop-setup) , and review the plan against real numbers once a quarter. Revenue per provider and rebooking rate belong on the same dashboard, which our[med spa KPI guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-kpi-tracking) lays out. If your plan pays only on volume, check that[rebooking and retention](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-retention-and-rebooking) do not slip, since those are the numbers a pure production incentive tends to push down.


## How Decoda Health Handles Commission Rules


Decoda Health builds the plan as rules: you choose the payee, the rate structure and what the percentage applies to, then assign each rule to the providers it covers. The[Decoda Health commissions module](https://decodahealth.com/products/commissions) supports three payee modes (the seller, the provider who delivers, or the staff member whose outbound contact preceded the booking), selectable per rule.


Tiers can be graduated or stepwise, set as percentages or flat amounts, and reset weekly, biweekly, monthly, quarterly, annually or never. Rules calculate net of discounts by default, can be switched to ignore discounts, and always exclude prepayment discounts so prepaid items pay in full. For packages, a rule can recognize the commission at the sale or at redemption, and a refunded redemption reverses the payout it created. A rule can cover all sales, a category, an item type or a single item, so injectables, retail and packages can each have their own terms.


At checkout in[Decoda Health billing](https://decodahealth.com/products/billing) , each line item has an editable Sold by field. By default it follows the provider on the appointment, and it can be set for a product sold with no appointment at all. It takes one person per item, so a plan that splits one line between two people needs a separate rule or a team bonus. Our[upselling guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-upselling-revenue-tips) covers the sales side of the same plan.


## Final Thoughts on Your Injector Commission Structure


Pick the percentage last. First settle what it applies to, whether tiers are graduated or stepwise, who is credited when the seller and the provider differ, and what a refund does to the payout. Write those four answers on one page, share it with your injectors before the next pay period, and test it against last month's real numbers.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What is a typical med spa injector commission structure?


Most med spas pay injectors an hourly or salaried base plus a percentage of the injectable revenue they produce. Published benchmarks vary widely, from about 10 to 20 percent in some guides to 25 to 40 percent in vendor reports, because they measure different things. Decide first whether the percentage applies to list price, discounted price or collected cash, then pick the rate.


Should med spa injector commission be tiered or flat?


A flat rate is easiest to explain and audit, while tiers reward volume and give a busy injector a reason to fill the schedule. If you tier, decide whether each band pays its own rate (graduated) or the top band reached applies to every sale (stepwise). The two plans can differ by thousands of dollars in the same month, so write the choice down.


Should commission be calculated before or after discounts?


Pay on the net price the patient actually paid unless you have a reason not to. A commission calculated on list price means the practice funds the discount and the commission on the discount at the same time. If you want injectors to be neutral about promotions, pay on list price and accept that cost knowingly, in writing.


Who gets commission when one person sells a package and another delivers the sessions?


You have to choose, because the software cannot guess. Paying the seller at the sale rewards closing, paying the provider at each redemption rewards delivery, and some clinics split the credit across both. Whichever you pick, refunds should reverse the payout they created, or the injector keeps pay on treatments that never happened.


Is paying an injector a percentage of Botox revenue legal?


It depends on the state. Some states restrict percentage-based pay tied to medical services under fee-splitting and corporate practice rules, and the answer can change with how the practice is owned. Check your state with a healthcare attorney before you publish a plan, and see our fee-splitting guide for how the rules differ by state.


Do commissions affect overtime pay for injectors?


For non-exempt employees, yes. Under 29 CFR 778.117, commissions count as pay for work time and have to be included in the regular rate used to calculate overtime. Exempt providers are paid differently, so confirm each person's classification with your accountant or employment counsel before you set the plan.
